<div><br>
</div>

<div>

</td>
<td style="WIDTH: auto; VERTICAL-ALIGN: top; align: left">
<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold"><a name="BUSINESS"><!--Anchor--></a>BUSINESS</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify"><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Overview</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our business segments are based on the organizational structure used by management for making operating and investment decisions and for assessing performance.&#160; Our reportable business segments are: (i) broadcasting; (ii) publishing; and (iii) corporate.&#160; Our broadcasting segment consists of 13 television stations and 35 radio stations in 11 states.&#160; Results from our digital media assets are included in our broadcasting and publishing segments.&#160; Our publishing segment consists of the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font>, which serves as the only major daily newspaper for the Milwaukee metropolitan area, and several community publications &#8211; primarily in southeastern Wisconsin &#8211; as well as print facilities in West Milwaukee and Waupaca, Wisconsin.&#160; Our corporate segment consists of unallocated corporate expenses and revenue eliminations.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We were founded in 1882 as a newspaper publisher serving Milwaukee, Wisconsin.&#160; Our media business mix was expanded in 1927 when we signed on radio station WTMJ-AM, and again in 1947 when we put WTMJ-TV on the air.&#160; In 1937, Harry J. Grant founded our employee ownership plan, which contributed significantly to our company&#8217;s positive culture and growth through its termination in 2003, in conjunction with our initial public offering.&#160; We believe our current capital structure allows us to continue our longstanding tradition of employee ownership.&#160; We have been able to attract and retain motivated people who have a passion for the business and a level of commitment and sense of accountability that is heightened due to our business culture and employees&#8217; ability to participate in ownership.&#160; Our culture is reinforced by our strong commitment to high ethical standards.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our revenue was $397.3 million, $393.1 million, and $351.5 million in 2013, 2012, and 2011, respectively.&#160; The revenue generated by our operating segments as a percentage of our consolidated revenue for the last three years is shown below:</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Broadcasting</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our broadcasting business is conducted through our wholly owned subsidiary, Journal Broadcast Corporation, and its subsidiaries, which together operate 13 television stations and 35 radio stations in 11 states.&#160; Our broadcasting business accounted for 61.3% of our revenue for the year ended December 29, 2013.&#160; See &#8220;Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; and Note 14, &#8220;Segment Reporting,&#8221; to our consolidated financial statements for additional financial information regarding our broadcasting business.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our radio and television stations focus on providing targeted and relevant local programming that is responsive to the interests of the communities in which we compete.&#160; We promote a local focus that allows our stations and radio clusters to serve listeners, viewers and advertisers effectively.&#160; Our local focus strengthens each station&#8217;s brand identity and allows our stations to provide effective marketing solutions for advertisers by reaching their targeted audiences.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In an effort to maximize our operating margins, we have implemented a centralized management approach to certain functions such as IT, billing, finance, purchasing and human resources to generate economies of scale and incorporate best practices.&#160; We intend to continue to pursue market share and invest in ratings growth which we believe will generate increased revenue and drive improvement in operating margin.&#160; We also plan to continue to diligently manage our expenses and make prudent investments to drive revenue.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The affiliation by a station with one of the four major networks (NBC, ABC, CBS and FOX) has a significant impact on the composition of the station&#8217;s programming, revenue, expenses and operations.&#160; Lower ratings of network programming can have an adverse affect on revenue.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We believe all of our television stations are strong affiliates with good relationships with the respective networks.&#160; In all of our markets and regardless of network affiliation, we focus on delivering leading local news programming, locally produced programming and contracting for popular syndicated programming with the objective of maximizing our ratings and, in turn, our share of advertising spending in a given market.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Political and issue and automotive advertising are our most significant broadcasting revenue categories.&#160; Television advertising revenue and rates in even-numbered years typically benefit from political and issue and Olympics advertising.&#160; As the demand for advertising increases on the limited available inventory, we have the opportunity to increase the average unit rates we charge our customers.&#160; Television political and issue advertising revenue was $1.3 million in 2013 compared to $34.0 million in 2012.&#160; NBC has purchased the right to broadcast the Olympics through 2020, which will benefit our NBC affiliates in 2014.&#160; Olympics-related advertising on our two NBC affiliates was $2.3 million in 2012.&#160; Automotive advertising revenue increased by $11.6 million, or 31.2%, in 2013 compared to 2012.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We currently have retransmission consent agreements with Multichannel Video Programming Distributors (MVPDs) in our local markets for the rights to distribute our signals and local programming in their pay television services to consumers.&#160; Our television stations experienced an $11.7 million, or 114.6%, increase in retransmission consent revenue in 2013 due to the acquisition of NewsChannel 5 Network, LLC, contractual annual rate increases and the&#160;renewal of several contracts.&#160; </font>These agreements are for multiple years with set rate increases and are based upon the number of subscribers to the MVPDs<font style="FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"> systems</font>.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify"><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We have made substantial investments in digital transmission equipment at our stations and are fully compliant with FCC mandates on digital transmission.&#160; We anticipate investing in digital infrastructure in several of our television markets as we make the continuing transition to HDTV (high-definition television).&#160; Also, we expect these investments to create additional operating efficiencies and improve the transfer of program content to our Internet websites.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Radio Broadcasting</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Based on the Fall 2013 Arbitron ratings book, we have the number one station in terms of station audience rank in two of the eight clusters in which our radio stations operate.&#160; We have grown our radio operations primarily through acquisitions of stations in mid-sized markets with growth potential.&#160; In 2013, revenue from radio operations accounted for 31.6% of our broadcasting revenue.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We employ a variety of sales-related and programming strategies.&#160; Our sales-related strategies include maximizing our share of the advertising spending.&#160; We believe development of local station clusters allows us to maximize market share because it allows us to offer a variety of format alternatives to appeal to a broader range of local advertisers.&#160; Our programming strategy includes developing and retaining local on-air talent to drive ratings.&#160; We have long-term contracts with many of our on-air personalities.&#160; In addition, our Milwaukee radio station, WTMJ-AM, currently maintains exclusive radio broadcast rights for the Green Bay Packers, Milwaukee Brewers and Milwaukee Bucks, and operates a statewide network for their games.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Most of our radio broadcasting revenue is generated from the sale of local advertising, which includes non-traditional advertising programs.&#160; Non-traditional advertising refers to initiatives which attract new local advertisers, including the creation of new local content and programs that combine television, radio or print with digital.&#160; The balance of broadcasting revenue is generated from the sale of national advertising, political and issue advertising and other sources.&#160; We have predetermined the number of commercials that are broadcast each hour, depending on the format of a particular station.&#160; We attempt to determine the number of commercials broadcast hourly that can maximize available revenue dollars without diminishing listening levels.&#160; Although the number of advertisements broadcast during a given time period may vary, the total number of advertisements broadcast on a particular station generally does not vary significantly from year to year, unless there has been a format change.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We have aligned our radio stations in clusters within a market, in many cases building out the cluster around a lead station.&#160; We seek to build a unique and differentiated brand position at each station within a cluster so that we can offer distinct solutions for a variety of advertisers in any given market.&#160; This clustering strategy has allowed us to target our stations&#8217; formats and sales efforts to better serve advertisers and listeners as well as leverage operating expenses to maximize the performance of each station and the cluster.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Industry and Competition</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We compete with other radio and television stations, newspapers, cable television, satellite television and radio, mobile, direct mail services, billboards and the Internet for advertising dollars.&#160; In the future, we may also compete with newer digital platforms including wireless Internet technology in the automobile.&#160; We believe some of the factors an advertiser considers when choosing an advertising medium include its overall marketing strategy and the ability to reach its targeted audience in the most cost-effective manner.&#160; In both radio and television broadcasting, revenue is derived primarily from advertising.&#160; Ratings, which estimate the number of listeners or viewers tuning in to a given station, highly influence competition in broadcasting because they affect the advertising rates the broadcaster can charge&#8212;higher ratings generally mean the broadcaster can charge higher rates for advertising.&#160; By having a cluster of several stations within one market, we can offer advertisers the opportunity to purchase air time on more than one of our stations in order to reach a broader audience.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">6</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Revenues in the broadcast industry are derived primarily from the sale of advertising time to local, national, political and issue advertisers, retransmission fees and, to a lesser extent, from barter, digital revenues and other sources.&#160; Because television and radio broadcasters rely upon advertising revenue, they are subject to cyclical changes in the economy.&#160; The size of advertisers&#8217; budgets, which are affected by broad economic trends, affects the radio industry in general and the revenue of individual television stations, in particular.&#160; Other than the political and issue and automotive categories, our broadcasting business continues to experience an uneven economic recovery across the markets in which we operate due to continued challenges in employment and the housing markets.&#160; Our broadcasting business also is affected by audience fragmentation as audiences have an increasing number of options to access news, syndicated programs and other programming.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Changes in market demographics, the entry of competitive stations, the adoption of competitive formats by existing stations and the inability to retain popular on-air talent could result in lower ratings, which could in turn reduce advertising revenue.&#160; Technology can play an important role in competition as the ratings each station receives also depend upon the strength of the station&#8217;s signal in each market and, therefore, the number of listeners who have access to the signal.&#160; We continue to invest in the technology needed to maintain, and, where possible, strengthen our signals.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Commercial television stations generally fall into one of three categories.&#160; The first category of stations includes those affiliated with one of the four major national networks (NBC, ABC, CBS and FOX).&#160; The second category includes stations affiliated with more recently developed national networks, such CW and MyNetwork TV (MNT).&#160; The third category includes independent stations that are not affiliated with any network and rely principally on local and syndicated programming.&#160; Affiliation with a television network can have a significant influence on the revenue of a television station because the audience ratings generated by a network&#8217;s programming can affect the rates at which a station can sell advertising time.&#160; Generally, each station determines rates and receives all of the revenue, net of agency commissions, for national and local spot advertising.&#160; Our retransmission revenue has increased significantly in recent years and we expect that retransmission revenue will continue to increase with annual contractual rate increases in our existing contracts with MVPDs and strategic renegotiation of expiring contracts.&#160; We renewed our network affiliation agreements with ABC, FOX, CW and MNT in 2011.&#160; We renewed our network affiliation agreement with NBC in 2013.&#160; The renewed network agreements include higher programming fees payable to the networks, which we expect will continue to increase.&#160; There can be no assurance that we will achieve and/or maintain profitability on our retransmission agreements after accounting for payments to networks.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Seasonal revenue fluctuations are common in the broadcasting industry and are primarily due to fluctuations in advertising expenditures by retailers and automobile manufacturers.&#160; Broadcast advertising is typically strongest in the second and fourth quarters of the year, which coincides with increased advertising around certain holidays.&#160; Historically, the second quarter tends to show an increase in automotive advertising as well as increases in tourism and travel advertising before the summer months.&#160; Television advertising revenue and rates in even-numbered years typically benefit from political and issue advertising because there tends to be more pressure on available inventory as the demand for advertising increases and we have the opportunity to increase average unit rates we charge our customers.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Publishing</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our publishing business is conducted through our wholly owned subsidiaries, Journal Sentinel, Inc. and Journal Community Publishing Group, Inc., and consists of our daily newspaper, the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font>, and our community publications.&#160; Our publishing business accounted for 38.9% of our revenue for the year ended December 29, 2013.&#160; Within our publishing segment, our daily newspaper accounted for 90.6% of our publishing revenue.&#160; See &#8220;Management&#8217;s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations&#8221; and Note 14, &#8220;Segment Reporting,&#8221; to our consolidated financial statements for additional financial information regarding our publishing business.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Daily Newspaper</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Published continuously since 1882, our daily newspaper has the largest circulation of any newspaper published in Wisconsin, with a six-month average net paid circulation reported to the Alliance for Audited Media in our Publisher&#8217;s Statement at September 30, 2013 of 318,711 on Sunday and 194,321 daily (on a five-day average).&#160; The <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font> serves as the only major daily and Sunday newspaper for the Milwaukee metropolitan area.&#160; According to a 2013 readership survey conducted by Scarborough Research, the daily and Sunday <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font> rank number one in readership among the 50 highest populated markets in the United States.&#160; Over the course of a week, readership of our print newspaper and digital websites combined ranks first among the largest U.S. markets with a 59% penetration rate.&#160; These rankings are calculated by dividing the number of adults reading an average issue of the newspaper in a newspaper&#8217;s Designated Market Area (DMA) by the number of persons over the age of 18 in the newspaper&#8217;s DMA. The <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font>&#8217;s DMA, which ranks among the top 50 in the United States, consists of the 10-county area surrounding Milwaukee, Wisconsin.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In 2011, our daily newspaper won its third Pulitzer Prize in four years for explanatory reporting. Only the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">New York Times</font> and the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Washington Post</font> have won journalism&#8217;s highest honor more times in those four years than the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font>.&#160;&#160; In 2008 and 2010, the <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font> received Pulitzers in the Local Reporting category.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">7</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In 2013, our newsroom staff received many awards for both print and digital coverage, from investigative work to features. Reporter Dan Egan was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize in Explanatory Reporting for his coverage of invasive species in the Great Lakes, work that also won the AAAS/Kavli Science Journalism Award and a National Headliner Award for environmental reporting. Our watchdog coverage of the Milwaukee Police Department &#8211; from questionable crime numbers to a death in police custody &#8211; won the Eugene Pulliam First Amendment Award from the Society of Professional Journalists and was named Best of Show in the Headliner Awards. Separately, the investigation into the police custody death of an alleged felon won a George Polk award, while an investigation into suspicious crime numbers received the Clark Mollenhoff Award. Our &#8220;Paper Cuts&#8221; series, exploring the decline of Wisconsin&#8217;s paper industry and the rise of China as a paper power, won the APME International Perspectives Award, the top SABEW award for explanatory reporting and was recognized for digital storytelling by the Society for Features Journalism. Other recognition included a Casey Medal for a story about a child&#8217;s sexual identity issues and a career achievement award for medical reporter John Fauber. The newspaper&#8217;s business section was recognized for general excellence by the Society of American Business &amp; Economics Writers (SABEW), our Tap Milwaukee website won an &#8220;Eppy&#8221; for best entertainment website and the &#8220;Wisconsin Voter&#8221; blog, written by Craig Gilbert, was named top news/political blog.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In addition to our traditional print media, we operate a number of websites that provide editorial and advertising content, including JSOnline.com, Milwaukeemoms.com and the MyCommunityNOW family of 26 community websites.&#160; Our daily newspaper operates a co-branded online automotive offering under a franchise agreement with CarSoup of Minnesota, Inc. (CarSoup.com).&#160; In 2013, online revenue of $12.8 million for digital products affiliated with our daily newspaper increased 3.7% compared to $12.3 million in 2012, primarily due to an increase in ads purchased through programmatic buying, real-time bidding and retail sponsorship ads.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Circulation revenue accounted for 34.9% of our daily newspaper&#8217;s total revenue in 2013.&#160; The <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font> single copy prices are $1.25 for daily, and $2.50 for Sunday, following a price increase for Sunday in June 2013 and for daily in July 2013, in our five county primary market area.&#160; We believe our average net paid print circulation will decrease due to, among other factors, increased competition for readers from new media products, other free sources and time pressures on consumers.&#160; Advertising revenue accounted for 52.5% of our daily newspaper&#8217;s total revenue in 2013.&#160; Our daily newspaper experienced decreased revenue in most print advertising categories in 2013 compared to 2012 due to the secular influences affecting the newspaper industry and the continued economic uncertainty.&#160; Digital advertising revenue and our Total Market Coverage (TMC) product showed growth in 2013 over 2012.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Milwaukee Journal Sentinel</font> introduced a digital subscription program, or &#8220;paywall,&#8221; on our jsonline.com website in January 2012.&#160; Integrated into the launch of the paywall was a price increase to our home delivery subscribers, who gain full access to all digital products with their subscription fee.</div>

<div>&#160;</div>

<div>Other revenue, which consists of commercial printing revenue, commercial distribution, and revenue from promotional events,&#160;accounted for 12.6% of our daily newspaper's total revenue in 2013.&#160; Our state-of-the-art printing facility, which now includes the ability to print ultra-violet coated pages, similar to magazines, allows us to leverage our existing assets to sign long term agreements to print other daily newspapers, such as <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">USA Today, Wall Street Journal, Kenosha News</font>, <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Pioneer Press </font>suburban editions<font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">, Chicago Reader</font> and others.&#160; We believe we provide high quality, competitive pricing and close proximity to their readers in southeastern Wisconsin and Chicago and its suburbs.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Community Publications</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We own and operate community publications and a printing plant in Waupaca, Wisconsin through our subsidiary, Journal Community Publishing Group, Inc. In December 2012, we sold all but two of our community publications in northern Wisconsin.&#160; The remaining publications are primarily in southeastern Wisconsin.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Lake Country Publications and its multi-media products captured a record 90 national and state awards, including the best-in-class trophy from the Wisconsin Newspaper Association for the largest weekly newspapers in 2013.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our community publications have a combined paid and free average weekly distribution of approximately 175,000. Our community publications focus on local news and events that are of interest to the local residents.&#160; In some markets, our community publications are the only source of local news.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We also publish a business-to-business publication that appeals to advertisers and readers in the agricultural market with a combined paid and free average monthly distribution of approximately 20,000.</div>

</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Newsprint</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The basic raw material of newspapers is newsprint.&#160; In 2013, we purchased the majority of our newsprint requirements through a purchasing agent, which has the option to purchase newsprint from multiple suppliers.&#160; We may purchase additional newsprint in the spot market from other suppliers.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We believe we will continue to receive an adequate supply of newsprint for our needs.&#160; Newsprint prices fluctuate based upon market factors, which include newsprint production capacity, currency exchange rates, manufacturer&#8217;s cost drivers, inventory levels, demand and consumption.&#160; Price fluctuations for newsprint can have a significant effect on our results of operations.&#160; The average net price per ton was $609 in 2013 compared to an average net price per ton of $629 in 2012, net of scrap sales.&#160; Our consumption of newsprint decreased to 23,113 metric tons in 2013 (52 weeks) from 24,880 metric tons in 2012 (53 weeks), and our total cost of newsprint decreased $1.6 million in 2013 compared to 2012.&#160; The decrease in consumption in 2013 at our publishing businesses was primarily due to decreases in average net paid circulation, run-of-press (ROP) advertising,&#160;and number of content pages. Based on the consumption of newsprint in 2013 by our daily newspaper and by our community publications, a $10 per ton increase or decrease in the price of newsprint would increase or decrease our total cost of newsprint by $0.2 million.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 36pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Industry and Competition</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Newspaper publishing was the first segment of the consumer media industry.&#160; Metropolitan and community publications often represent the primary medium for news and local advertising due to their historic importance to the communities they serve.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In recent years, newspaper industry fundamentals have declined as a result of the 2009 recession and secular industry change. Based on our results, we believe the rate of decline moderated in 2013.&#160; Retail and classified ROP advertising have decreased from historic levels due in part to department store consolidation, weakened employment, automotive and real estate economics and a migration of advertising to the Internet and other advertising forms.&#160; Circulation declines and online competition have also negatively impacted newspaper industry revenues.&#160; Additionally, the housing market downturn, while now showing signs of recovery, has adversely impacted the newspaper industry, including real estate classified advertising as well as the home improvement, furniture and financial services advertising categories.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Advertising revenue is the largest component of a newspaper&#8217;s total revenue and it is affected by cyclical changes in national and regional economic conditions, as well as secular changes in the newspaper industry.&#160; Classified advertising is generally the most sensitive to economic cycles and secular changes in the newspaper business because it is driven primarily by the demand for employment, real estate transactions and automotive sales, as well as the migration of advertising to the Internet and other advertising forms.&#160; Classified revenue&#8217;s share has fallen to 19% of total publishing advertising revenues.&#160; Newspaper advertising revenue is seasonal and our publishing business tends to see increased revenue due to increased advertising activity during certain holidays.&#160; We do not expect that revenues at our daily newspaper or community publications will return to revenue levels reported in 2012 or prior years given the secular changes affecting the newspaper industry.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">We believe newspapers and their online and niche products continue to be one of the most effective mediums for retail and classified advertising because they allow advertisers to promote the price and selection of goods more timely than most broadcast media, and to maximize household reach within a local retail trading area.&#160; This is especially true in a market like Milwaukee, which is still home to a number of local-market decision makers who influence spending to reach shoppers in this community.&#160; Notwithstanding the advertising advantages newspapers offer, newspapers have many competitors for advertising dollars and paid circulation.&#160; These competitors include local, regional and national newspapers, shoppers, magazines, broadcast and cable television, radio, direct mail, Yellow Pages, the Internet, mobile devices and other media.&#160; Competition for newspaper advertising revenue is based largely upon advertiser results, advertising rates, readership, demographics and circulation levels, while competition for circulation revenue is based largely upon the content of the newspaper, its price, editorial quality and customer service.&#160; On occasion, our businesses compete with each other for regional and local advertising, particularly in the Milwaukee market.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Compliance with Environmental Laws</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">As the owner, lessee or operator of various real properties and facilities, we are subject to various federal, state and local environmental laws and regulations.&#160; Historically, compliance with these laws and regulations has not had a material adverse effect on our business.&#160; Compliance with existing or new environmental laws and regulations may require us to make future expenditures.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Regulation</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Our television and radio businesses are subject to regulation by governmental authorities in the United States.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; MARGIN-LEFT: 18pt"><!--Anchor--><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Introduction</font></div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><a name="_DV_M7"><!--Anchor--></a>Our television and radio broadcasting operations are subject to regulation by the FCC under the Communications Act of 1934, as amended (which we refer to as the Communications Act).&#160; Under authority of the Communications Act, the FCC, among other things, assigns frequency bands for broadcast and other uses; determines the location, frequency and operating power of stations; grants permits and licenses to construct and operate television and radio stations on particular frequencies; issues, revokes, modifies and renews radio and television broadcast station licenses; regulates equipment used by stations; determines whether to approve changes in ownership or control of station licenses; regulates the content of some forms of programming; adopts and implements regulations and policies which directly or indirectly affect the ownership, operations and profitability of broadcasting stations; and has the power to impose penalties for violations of its rules.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><a name="_DV_M8"><!--Anchor--></a>Licensed broadcast stations must pay FCC regulatory and application fees and comply with various rules promulgated under the Communications Act that regulate, among other things, political advertising, sponsorship identification, closed captioning of certain television programming, obscene, indecent and profane broadcasts, and technical operations, including limits on radio frequency radiation.&#160; Additionally, the FCC&#8217;s rules require licensees to implement equal employment opportunity outreach programs and maintain records and make filings with the FCC evidencing such efforts.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><a name="_DV_M9"><!--Anchor--></a>The following is a brief summary of certain provisions of the Communications Act and specific FCC rules and policies.&#160; The summaries are not intended to describe all present and proposed statutes and FCC rules and regulations that impact our television and radio operations.&#160; Failure to observe the provisions of the Communications Act and the FCC&#8217;s rules and policies can result in the imposition of various sanctions, including monetary forfeitures, the grant of &#8220;short-term&#8221; (less than the maximum term) license renewals or, for particularly egregious violations, the denial of a license renewal application, the revocation of a license or the withholding of approval for acquisition of additional broadcast properties.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; MARGIN-LEFT: 18pt; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Broadcast Licenses/Renewals</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Communications Act permits the operation of a broadcast station only in accordance with a license issued by the FCC upon a finding that the grant of a license would serve the public interest, convenience and necessity.&#160; The FCC grants broadcast licenses for specified periods of time and, upon application, may renew the licenses for additional terms (ordinarily for the full term of eight years).&#160; Generally, the FCC renews a broadcast license upon a finding that (i) the broadcast station has served the public interest, convenience and necessity; (ii) there have been no serious violations by the licensee of the Communications Act or the FCC&#8217;s rules; and (iii) there have been no other violations by the licensee of the Communications Act or other FCC rules which, taken together, indicate a pattern of abuse.&#160; After considering these factors, the FCC may renew a broadcast station&#8217;s license, either with conditions or without, or it may designate the renewal application for hearing.&#160; Although there can be no assurance that our licenses will be renewed, we have not to date had a violation of the FCC&#8217;s regulations that jeopardized the renewal of our licenses, and we are not currently aware of any facts that would prevent their renewal.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On November 1, 2005, the Milwaukee Public Interest Media Coalition (&#8220;MPIMC&#8221;) filed a petition at the FCC asking it to deny the pending license renewal applications of all eleven commercial television stations in the Milwaukee Designated Market Area (DMA), including our station, WTMJ-TV, on the grounds that the stations failed to provide adequate coverage of state and local issues during the 2004 election campaign.&#160; In June 2007, the FCC issued an Order denying MPIMC&#8217;s Petition.&#160; In July 2007, MPIMC filed a Petition for Reconsideration with the FCC requesting it to reconsider the denial of MPIMC&#8217;s Petition to Deny.&#160; We opposed MPIMC&#8217;s Petition for Reconsideration and in July 2008, the FCC issued a decision denying the Petition for Reconsideration.&#160; In August 2008, MPIMC filed a second Petition for Reconsideration of the FCC&#8217;s June 2007 Order.&#160; We filed an Opposition to MPIMC&#8217;s Second Petition in August 2008.&#160; The FCC dismissed MPIMC&#8217;s Second Petition on January 12, 2009.&#160; On February 16, 2010, MPIMC filed an Application for Review requesting the FCC to review the dismissal of MPIMC&#8217;s Second Petition.&#160; We filed an Opposition to MPIMC&#8217;s Application for Review jointly with several other television stations in the Milwaukee DMA, and MPIMC filed a Reply.&#160; By letter dated December 10, 2010, the FCC dismissed MPIMC&#8217;s Application for Review.&#160; On January 10, 2011, MPIMC filed another Application for Review requesting the FCC to vacate its December 10, 2010 order and consider MPIMC&#8217;s February 10, 2010 Application for Review on its merits.&#160; On January 25, 2011, we filed an Opposition to the second Application for Review jointly with several other Milwaukee television station licensees.&#160; MPIMC filed a consolidated Reply to the Joint Opposition on February 2, 2011.&#160; The matter remains pending.</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: left; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">On October 29, 2012, Media Action Center filed a Petition to Deny the renewal application of Station WTMJ(AM), Milwaukee, WI, alleging that the Station violated FCC rules because it did not provide sufficient time to supporters of certain candidates for state office.&#160; On November 28, 2012, Journal filed an Opposition to the Petition.&#160; Media Action Center filed a response to Journal&#8217;s Opposition on December 18, 2012.&#160; The matter remains pending.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">10</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Ownership Restrictions</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Communications Act and FCC rules and policies include a number of limitations regarding the number and reach of broadcast stations that any person or entity may own, directly or by attribution.&#160; FCC approval is also required for transfers of control and assignments of station licenses.&#160; A person or entity requesting FCC approval to acquire a radio or television station license must demonstrate that the acquisition complies with the FCC&#8217;s ownership rules or that a waiver of the rules is in the public interest.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The FCC is required to review quadrennially the following media ownership rules and to modify, repeal or retain any rules as it determines to be in the public interest: the newspaper broadcast cross-ownership rule; the local radio ownership rule; the radio-television cross-ownership rule; the dual network rule; and the local television ownership rule.&#160; In 2008, the FCC released a Report and Order that modified only the newspaper broadcast cross-ownership rule to permit cross-ownership of one newspaper and one television or radio station in the top twenty markets under certain circumstances, and establishing a waiver procedure for such combinations in markets smaller than the top twenty.&#160; The FCC stated that newspaper broadcast combinations that were grandfathered in 1975 when the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rule was adopted, including our Milwaukee operations, will continue to be grandfathered.&#160; In a decision issued on July 7, 2011, the Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit vacated and remanded the modified newspaper broadcast cross-ownership rule.&#160; A Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (&#8220;Ownership NPRM&#8221;) with respect to its 2010 quadrennial review of the media ownership rules that proposes to modify the newspaper broadcast cross-ownership rule to apply a positive presumption to requests to own a daily newspaper and a broadcast station in the 20 largest DMAs if certain conditions are met and to repeal the radio television cross-ownership rule is currently pending.&#160; The FCC&#8217;s ownership rules that are currently in effect are briefly summarized below.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Newspaper-Broadcast Cross-Ownership Rule.&#160; </font>Under the currently effective newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership Rule, unless grandfathered or subject to waiver, no party can have an attributable interest in both a daily English-language newspaper and either a television station or a radio station in the same market if specified signal contours of the television station or the radio station encompass the entire community in which the newspaper is published.&#160; Our media operations in Milwaukee are grandfathered under this rule.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Local Radio Ownership Rule.&#160; </font>The local radio ownership rule limits the number of radio stations an entity may own in a given market depending on the size of the radio market.&#160; Specifically, in a radio market with 45 or more commercial and noncommercial radio stations, a party may own, operate, or control up to eight commercial radio stations, not more than five of which are in the same service (AM or FM).&#160; In a radio market with between 30 and 44 radio stations, a party may own, operate, or control up to seven commercial radio stations, not more than four of which are in the same service.&#160; In a radio market with between 15 and 29 radio stations, a party may own, operate, or control up to six commercial radio stations, not more than four of which are in the same service.&#160; In a radio market with 14 or fewer radio stations, a party may own, operate, or control up to five commercial radio stations, not more than three of which are in the same service, except that a party may not own, operate, or control more than 50% of the stations in the market, except for combinations of one AM and one FM station, which are permitted in any size market.&#160; For stations located in a market in which the Arbitron ratings service provides ratings, the definition of &#8220;radio market&#8221; is based on the radio market to which BIA Kelsey reports assign the affected radio stations.&#160; For stations that are not in an Arbitron market, the market definition is based on technical service areas, pending further FCC rulemaking.&#160; Also under the rule, a radio station that provides more than 15% of another in-market station&#8217;s weekly programming or sells more than 15% of another in-market station&#8217;s weekly advertising will be deemed to have an attributable interest in the brokered station.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Radio-Television Cross-Ownership Rule.&#160; </font>The radio-television cross-ownership rule generally allows common ownership of one or two television stations and up to six radio stations, or, in certain circumstances, one television station and seven radio stations, in any market where at least 20 independent voices would remain after the combination; two television stations and up to four radio stations in a market where at least 10 independent voices would remain after the combination; and one television and one radio station notwithstanding the number of independent voices in the market.&#160; A &#8220;voice&#8221; generally includes independently owned, same-market commercial and noncommercial broadcast television and radio stations, newspapers of certain minimum circulation, and one cable system per market.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Local Television Ownership Rule.&#160; </font>Under the local television ownership rule, one party may own, operate, or control up to two television stations in a market, so long as the market would have at least eight independently owned full power television stations after the combination and at least one of the stations is not one of the top-four-rated stations (based on audience share) in the television market.&#160; The rule also permits the ownership, operation or control of two television stations in a market as long as the stations&#8217; Noise Limited Service contours do not overlap.&#160; In 2011, the FCC sought comments on its proposal to eliminate the contour overlap exception that permits common ownership of two television stations in the same market.&#160; The matter remains pending.&#160; The FCC may waive this rule to permit ownership, operation or control of two television stations in a market that will not otherwise be permissible if one of the stations is in involuntary bankruptcy, is a &#8220;failed&#8221; station, or is &#8220;failing&#8221; (i.e., stations with negative cash flow and less than a four share all day audience rating).&#160; Under the rule, the licensee of a television station that provides more than 15% of another in-market station&#8217;s weekly programming will be deemed to have an attributable interest in the other station.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">11</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Dual Network Rule.&#160; </font>The dual network rule prohibits any of the four major networks &#8212; ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC &#8212; from merging with each other.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Television National Audience Reach Limitation. </font>A person or entity is prohibited from having an attributable interest in television stations whose aggregate audience reach exceeds 39% of the television households in the United States.&#160; The FCC is precluded by statute from modifying this rule in connection with its mandated quadrennial review of the ownership rules.&#160; In calculating the number of households a station reaches, the FCC attributes a UHF station with only 50% of the television households in the market.&#160; In 2013, the FCC released a rulemaking proceeding proposing to eliminate the UHF discount which remains pending.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Attribution of Ownership.&#160; A</font>n &#8220;attributable&#8221; interest for purposes of the FCC&#8217;s broadcast ownership rules generally includes: (i) equity and debt interests which combined exceed 33% of a licensee&#8217;s total assets, if the interest holder supplies more that 15% of the licensee&#8217;s total weekly programming, or has an attributable same-market media interest, whether television, radio, cable or newspaper; (ii) a 5% or greater direct or indirect voting stock interest, including certain interests held in trust, unless the holder is a qualified passive investor in which case the threshold is a 20% or greater voting stock interest; (iii) any equity interest in a limited liability company or a partnership, including a limited partnership, unless properly &#8220;insulated&#8221; from management activities; and (iv) any position as an officer or director of a licensee or of its direct or indirect parent.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Alien Ownership</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The Communications Act restricts the ability of foreign entities or individuals to own or hold interests in U.S. broadcast licenses.&#160; Foreign governments, representatives of foreign governments, non-U.S. citizens, representatives of non-U.S. citizens, and corporations or partnerships organized under the laws of a foreign country (collectively, &#8220;aliens&#8221;) are prohibited from holding broadcast licenses.&#160; Aliens may directly or indirectly own or vote, in the aggregate, up to 20% of the capital stock of a licensee.&#160; In addition, a broadcast license may not be granted to or held by any corporation that is controlled, directly or indirectly, by any other corporation more than 25% of whose capital stock is owned or voted by aliens if the FCC finds that the public interest will be served by the refusal or revocation of such license.&#160; The FCC has interpreted this provision to require an affirmative finding that foreign ownership in excess of 25% would serve the public interest and, in the past, the FCC has made such an affirmative finding in the broadcast context only in highly limited circumstances.&#160; In 2013, however, the FCC issued a declaratory ruling that notwithstanding its past practices it will consider on a case-by-case basis requests for approval of acquisitions by aliens of in excess of 25% of the stock of the parent of a broadcast licensee.&#160; In acting upon such a request, the FCC will coordinate with Executive Branch agencies on national security, law enforcement, foreign policy, and trade policy issues.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Repurposing of Broadcast Spectrum for Other Uses</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In February 2012, Congress passed and the President signed legislation that, among other things, grants the FCC authority to conduct incentive auctions to recapture certain spectrum currently used by television broadcasters and repurpose it for other uses.&#160; On October 2, 2012, the FCC released a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking to begin to develop the rules and procedures to implement incentive auctions authorized by Congress.&#160; That rulemaking process remains ongoing.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The incentive auction process would have three components.&#160; First, the FCC would conduct a reverse auction by which each television broadcaster may choose to retain its rights to a 6 MHz channel of spectrum or volunteer, in return for payment, to relinquish all of the station&#8217;s spectrum by surrendering its license; relinquish the right to some of its spectrum and thereafter share spectrum with another station; or modify its UHF channel license to a VHF channel license.&#160; Second, in order to accommodate the spectrum reallocated to new users, the FCC will &#8220;repack&#8221; the remaining television broadcast spectrum, which may require certain television stations that did not participate in the reverse auction to modify their transmission facilities, including requiring such stations to operate on different channels.&#160; The FCC has solicited comments on various aspects of the repacking and reimbursement process.&#160; The FCC is authorized to reimburse stations for reasonable relocation costs up to a total across all stations of $1.75 billion.&#160; In addition, Congress directed the FCC, when repacking television broadcast spectrum, to make reasonable efforts to preserve a station&#8217;s coverage area and population served.&#160; Also, the FCC is prohibited from requiring a station to move involuntarily from the UHF band to the VHF band or from the high VHF band to the low VHF band.&#160; The statute does not protect low power stations in the repacking process.&#160; Third, the FCC would conduct a forward auction of the relinquished spectrum to new users.&#160; The FCC must complete the reverse auction and the forward auction by September 30, 2022, and has announced that as of now it intends to conduct the auction during 2015.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The outcome of the incentive auction and repacking of broadcast television spectrum, or the impact of such items on our business, cannot be predicted.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">12</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Obscenity, Indecency and Profanity</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The FCC's rules prohibit the broadcast of obscene material at any time and indecent or profane material between the hours of 6:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.&#160; In recent years, the FCC has intensified its enforcement activities with respect to programming it considers indecent and has issued numerous fines to licensees found to have violated the indecency rules.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In July 2007, the FCC implemented increased forfeiture amounts for indecency violations that were enacted by Congress. The maximum permitted fine for an indecency violation is $325,000 per incident and $3,000,000 for any continuing violation arising from a single act or failure to act.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Because the FCC may investigate indecency complaints on an <font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">ex parte</font> basis, a licensee may not have knowledge of an indecency complaint unless and until the complaint results in the issuance of a formal FCC letter of inquiry or notice of apparent liability for forfeiture.&#160; From time to time, our television and radio stations receive letters of inquiry and notices of proposed forfeitures from the FCC alleging that they have broadcast indecent material.&#160; We do not believe that broadcasts identified in any currently pending complaints of which we are aware violate the indecency standards.&#160; In July 2010, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit issued a decision finding that the FCC&#8217;s indecency standard was too vague for broadcasters to interpret and therefore inconsistent with the First Amendment.&#160; In June 2012, the Supreme Court issued a decision which held that the FCC could not fine ABC and FOX for the specific broadcasts at issue in the case because the FCC had not provided them with sufficient notice of its intent to issue fines for the use of fleeting expletives.&#160; However, the Court did not make any substantive ruling regarding the FCC&#8217;s indecency standards.&#160; In April 2013, the FCC requested comments on its indecency policy, including whether it should ban the use of fleeting expletives or whether it should only impose fines for broadcasts that involve repeated and deliberate use of expletives.&#160; The FCC has not issued any decisions regarding indecency enforcement since the Supreme Court&#8217;s decision was issued although it has advised that it will continue to pursue enforcement actions in egregious cases while it conducts its review of its indecency policies generally.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Sponsorship Identification</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Both the Communications Act and the FCC&#8217;s rules generally require that, when payment or other consideration has been received or promised to a broadcast licensee for the airing of program material, the station must disclose that fact and identify who paid or promised to provide the consideration at the time of broadcast.&#160; In response to a complaint by a public interest organization, the FCC issued letters of inquiry to several dozen television stations seeking to determine whether their broadcast of &#8220;video news releases&#8221; (VNRs) violated the sponsorship identification rules by failing to disclose the source and sponsorship of the VNR materials.&#160; VNRs are news stories and feature materials produced by government agencies and commercial entities, among others, for use by broadcasters.&#160; Two of our television stations received and have responded to the VNR letter of inquiry.&#160; We cannot predict the outcome of the FCC&#8217;s investigation; however in 2007, the FCC issued a forfeiture notice to one cable company for alleged violations of the sponsorship identification rules based on the use of VNRs.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Digital Television</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">As of June 12, 2009, all full-power broadcast television stations were required to cease broadcasting analog programming and convert to all digital broadcasts.&#160; Digital broadcasting permits stations to offer digital channels for a wide variety of services such as high definition video programming, multiple channels of standard definition video programming, audio, data, and other types of communications.&#160; Each station is required to provide at least one free over-the-air video program signal.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">To the extent a station has &#8220;excess&#8221; digital capacity (i.e., digital capacity not used to transmit free, over-the-air video programming), it may elect to use that capacity in any manner consistent with FCC technical requirements, including for additional free program streams, data transmission, digital or subscription video services, or paging and information services.&#160; If a station uses its digital capacity to provide any services on a subscription or otherwise &#8220;feeable&#8221; basis, it must pay the FCC an annual fee equal to 5% of the gross revenues realized from such services.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Relationship with MVPDs</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">A number of provisions of the Communications Act and FCC rules govern aspects of the relationship between broadcast television stations and distributors of multiple channels of video programming such as cable, satellite and telecommunications companies (referred to as MVPDs).&#160; The rules generally provide certain protections for broadcast stations, for which MVPDs are an important means of distribution and a provider of competing program channels.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">To ensure that every local television station can be received in its local market without requiring a cable subscriber to switch between cable and off-air signals, the FCC allows every full-power television broadcast station to require that all local cable systems transmit that station&#8217;s primary digital channel to their subscribers within the station&#8217;s market (the so-called &#8220;must-carry&#8221; rule).&#160; Alternatively, a station may elect to forego its must-carry rights and seek a negotiated agreement to establish the terms of its carriage by a local cable system&#8212;referred to as &#8220;retransmission consent.&#8221;&#160; A station electing retransmission consent assumes the risk that it will not be able to strike a deal with the MVPD and will not be carried.&#160; A station has the opportunity to elect must-carry or retransmission consent every three years.&#160; Elections were made in October 2011 for the 2012-2014 three year period.&#160; We have elected retransmission consent rather than must carry with MVPDs for most of our television stations.&#160; A station that fails to notify a cable system of its election is presumed to have elected must-carry.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">13</div>

<hr style="PAGE-BREAK-AFTER: always; BORDER-RIGHT-WIDTH: 0px; BACKGROUND-COLOR: #000000; MARGIN: 4px 0px; WIDTH: 100%; BORDER-TOP-WIDTH: 0px; BORDER-BOTTOM-WIDTH: 0px; HEIGHT: 2px; COLOR: #000000; CLEAR: both; BORDER-LEFT-WIDTH: 0px" id="DSPFPageBreak" noshade="noshade">
<div style="WIDTH: 100%" id="DSPFPageHeader"><a style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" href="#INDEX">Index</a></div>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">Cable systems are not required to carry any programming streams other than a station&#8217;s primary video programming channel. Consequently, the multicast programming streams provided by several of our television stations are not entitled to mandatory carriage pursuant to the digital must-carry rules.&#160; However, because the FCC&#8217;s action does not affect digital retransmission consent agreements, we are free to negotiate with cable operators for the carriage of additional programming streams under mutually agreed terms and conditions.&#160; A similar must-carry and retransmission consent regime governs carriage of local broadcast channels by direct-to-home satellite television operators.&#160; A satellite provider is not required to transmit the signal of any television station to its subscribers in that station&#8217;s market.&#160; However, if a satellite provider chooses to provide one local station to its subscribers in a market, the provider also must transmit locally every other station in that market that elects must-carry status.&#160; As with cable, stations may opt to pursue retransmission consent agreements.&#160; A local television station that fails to make any election to a satellite provider is deemed to have elected retransmission consent and is not guaranteed carriage.&#160; Satellite must-carry election periods occur every three years, consistent with cable must-carry periods.&#160; We have elected retransmission consent with satellite television operators for all of our stations.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">In February 2011, the FCC issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (&#8220;NPRM&#8221;) reviewing the retransmission consent rules.&#160; The NPRM requests comment on proposals to strengthen the good faith negotiation requirements and to require advance notice of the potential that a television station could be dropped from an MVPD&#8217;s programming lineup.&#160; In a separate proceeding, the FCC has requested comment on whether the definition of MVPD should be expanded to include entities that make available multiple channels of video programming to subscribers through Internet connections.&#160; Both proceedings are pending, and we cannot predict what impact, if any, they will have on our negotiations with video programming distributors.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Children&#8217;s Television Programming</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt"><font style="FONT-STYLE: italic; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">&#160;</font>Federal legislation and FCC rules limit the amount and content of commercial matter that may be shown on television stations during programming designed for children 12 years and younger, and require stations to broadcast three hours per week of educational and informational programming (&#8220;E/I programming&#8221;) designed for children 16 years of age and younger.&#160; FCC rules also require television stations to broadcast E/I programming on each additional digital multicast program stream transmitted, with the requirement increasing in proportion to the additional hours of free programming offered on multicast channels.&#160; These rules also limit the display during children&#8217;s programming of Internet addresses of websites that contain or link to commercial material or that use program characters to sell products.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Digital Radio</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">The FCC permits existing AM and FM radio broadcast stations to broadcast digitally in order both to improve sound quality and to provide spectrum for multicast channels and/or enhanced data services to complement the existing programming service.&#160; The FCC has authorized AM and FM radio stations to broadcast digital signals using excess spectrum within the same allotted bandwidth used for analog transmissions.&#160; In January 2010, the FCC adopted procedures that allow FM radio stations to significantly increase their digital power levels above those originally permitted in order to improve the digital service these stations provide.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Closed Captioning</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">FCC rules require the majority of programming broadcast by television stations to contain closed captions.&#160; The FCC forwards to television stations viewer complaints it receives with respect to closed captioning problems, and several of our stations have received complaints that were filed with the FCC.&#160; We have responded to these complaints, and they are currently pending.&#160; In January 2012, the FCC adopted rules to require that television programming broadcast or transmitted with captioning include captioning of programming subsequently made available online, for example, by streaming content on broadcasters&#8217; websites.&#160; In 2013, the FCC released a rulemaking seeking comments regarding whether the Internet video captioning obligations should apply to brief segments or clips of video programs that are carried on the Internet.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">FCC rules also require, in part, that affiliates of the top-four national broadcast networks in the top 25 markets provide a minimum of 50 hours of video-described primetime and/or children&#8217;s programming each calendar quarter.&#160; The requirement to provide video descriptions will ultimately be expanded in 2015 to network affiliates in the top 60 markets.</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-STYLE: italic; TEXT-INDENT: 18pt; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt; FONT-WEIGHT: bold">Commercial Advertisement Loudness Mitigation</div>

<div><br>
</div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: justify; FONT-FAMILY: ''Times New Roman'', Times, serif; FONT-SIZE: 10pt">New rules enacted by the FCC that require our television broadcast stations to transmit commercials and adjacent programming at the same volume went into effect in December 2012.</div>

<div style="MARGIN-TOP: 10pt; MARGIN-BOTTOM: 10pt; CLEAR: both" id="DSPFPageBreakArea">
<div id="DSPFPageFooter"></div>

<div style="TEXT-ALIGN: center; FONT-FAMILY: 'Times New Roman', Times, Serif; COLOR: #000000; FONT-SIZE: 8pt" id="DSPFPageNumberArea">14</div>
